vignette:
Mrs. Lien is a seventy-one-year-old woman who sits very straight in the chair, her small hands folded in her lap. She is a retired financial analyst, and she still dresses for the office: a pressed silk blouse, tailored slacks, low heels. She apologizes twice for the traffic on the way here. She has been divorced for twenty-two years and lives alone in a condominium she owns outright. She says she does not need much.

She was thirty-four years old when the war came to her city. She does not say which war. She does not name the country. She says only, "The soldiers came." She was a junior accountant then, working for a state-owned enterprise. She was taken from her desk. She remembers the sun through the venetian blinds, the dust motes floating, the telephone ringing on a desk she would never sit at again. They kept her for eleven months.

She does not describe the physical conditions in detail. She says, "There was a room. There was a bucket. There was a man with a radio." She says the radio was always on, always tuned to static. The static would hiss for hours, and then a voice would speak, and then the static would return. She learned to listen for the voice because it meant the beating would stop. When the voice stopped, the beating resumed. She learned to pray for the voice.

She was not tortured for information. She was tortured because she was there. She was a symbol, she says. A symbol of what, she does not know. Perhaps of the old regime, perhaps of the new. She never understood the politics. She understood only that her body was a place where other people's anger lived.

She was released in a prisoner exchange. She weighed ninety-two pounds. Her hair had turned white. She returned to her desk, but the telephone no longer rang for her. She emigrated six years later, alone. Her husband had remarried. She does not blame him. She says, "He was a good man. He needed a wife who could sleep."

Now, at seventy-one, she cannot sleep. She goes to bed at ten and wakes at two, every night, without fail. She does not fight it. She gets up, makes tea, opens her laptop. She reviews spreadsheets from her retirement accounts. She finds the numbers soothing. They are predictable. They add up. She says she has not had a nightmare in years, but she corrects herself: "No. That is not true. I have nightmares, but I do not remember them. I wake up and my heart is fast. I know I was somewhere. But I do not know where. I do not want to know."

She avoids loud noises. She avoids crowds. She avoids the smell of diesel fuel. She avoids men in uniform, though she knows this is unfair. She avoids the news. She avoids any film or book that shows a room with a single lightbulb hanging from a wire. She has built her life around avoidance. She says it works. She says, "I have a good life. I have my tea. I have my numbers. I have my cat."

But her body remembers. Her hands tremble when she is startled. Her jaw is tight. She has a chronic pain in her left shoulder that no doctor can explain. She says it feels like a hand, pressing. She says it started in the room. She says it never left.

She came to therapy because her daughter, who lives in another state, told her she seemed "far away." Mrs. Lien did not understand. She said, "I am right here." Her daughter said, "No, Mom. You are not."

She is not sure what she wants from me. She is not sure she wants anything. She is here because she is a good mother, and a good mother tries. She sits very straight in her chair. She tells her story without tears. She says, "I survived. That is what I do."

But when I ask her what she feels when she thinks of the room, she is quiet for a long time. Then she says, "I feel nothing. That is the problem, isn't it? I feel nothing at all."

She looks down at her hands. They are still. She says, "I think the feeling part of me died in that room. And the rest of me just kept walking."
